content: People with cystic fibrosis (CF) suffer from chronic airway infections due to the accumulation of mucus in their lungs. These repeated infections often lead to lung damage and progressive lung disease. Airway clearance therapies are designed to help clear mucus, increase sputum production, and improve overall airway function. The active cycle of breathing technique (ACBT) is one such method. It involves a sequence of techniques, including controlled breathing, thoracic expansion exercises, and the forced expiration technique, to help loosen and clear airway secretions. This review aimed to evaluate the clinical effectiveness of ACBT compared to other airway clearance therapies for individuals with CF. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis Trials Register, clinical trial registries, and reference lists of relevant articles. The last search was conducted on March 29, 2021. They included randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials, including cross-over studies, that compared ACBT with other airway clearance methods. Two independent reviewers screened the studies, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias. The quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach, focusing on outcomes such as quality of life, participant preference, adverse events, lung function (measured by forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) % predicted and forced vital capacity (FVC) % predicted), sputum weight, and the number of pulmonary exacerbations. The search identified 99 studies, of which 22 met the inclusion criteria, involving a total of 559 participants. Eight of these studies (259 participants) were included in the analysis, with five using a cross-over design. The remaining 14 studies were cross-over studies but lacked sufficient reporting for full assessment. The sample sizes ranged from seven to 65 participants, with ages ranging from six to 63 years (mean age 18.7 years). Most studies had a follow-up period of only one day, although two long-term randomized controlled trials followed participants for one to three years. Many studies did not adequately report key methodological details, such as random sequence generation, allocation concealment, and blinding of outcome assessors, leading to an unclear risk of bias. Due to the nature of the intervention, participants and personnel were not blinded in any of the studies. However, most studies reported all planned outcomes, had adequate follow-up, assessed compliance, and used an intention-to-treat analysis. The included studies compared ACBT with various other airway clearance techniques, including autogenic drainage, airway oscillating devices (AOD), high-frequency chest compression devices, conventional chest physiotherapy (CCPT), positive expiratory pressure (PEP), and exercise. The findings showed no significant differences in quality of life between ACBT and PEP mask therapy, AOD, other breathing techniques, or exercise. Similarly, there was no difference in individual preference between ACBT and other techniques. These findings were based on very low-certainty evidence. One study that compared ACBT with ACBT plus postural exercise reported no deaths or adverse events, but the evidence was of very low certainty. There were no significant differences in lung function (FEV1 % predicted and FVC % predicted), oxygen saturation, or sputum weight between ACBT and other techniques. Additionally, there were no differences in the number of pulmonary exacerbations between individuals using ACBT and those using CCPT (low-certainty evidence) or ACBT combined with exercise (very low-certainty evidence). In conclusion, there is limited evidence to support or refute the use of ACBT over other airway clearance therapies. ACBT appears to be comparable to other techniques in terms of participant preference, quality of life, exercise tolerance, lung function, sputum weight, oxygen saturation, and the number of pulmonary exacerbations. Longer-term studies are needed to better evaluate the impact of ACBT on outcomes that are important to individuals with cystic fibrosis, such as quality of life and personal preference.
